title: Nineteen Universities and Seven Kingdoms: the Wandering Master of Artificial Memory
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Kues on the Mosel, and the Schools of Cologne

stops.name: Bernkastel-Kues, the son of Petrus Henklen
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: no birth entry exists. A library authority file assigns 1480; the Mosel origin comes from the 1529 Cracow faculty record naming his father Petrus Henklen of Kues, diocese of Trier
stops.campa: On the Mosel, in the diocese of Trier, a boy is born to Petrus Henklen of Kues. Nothing local keeps him: no baptismal entry, no house, no date, no godparent's name. He reaches the written record only about forty-nine years later, at Cracow, in the long form a faculty clerk takes down from his own dictation, Johannes Kusanus son of Petrus Henklen of Kues of the diocese of Trier. A cataloguer working backward from that line assigns him a birth around 1480. From the town on the river he takes the second name he will carry for the rest of his life.
suggested_refs: Kues on the Mosel, diocese of Trier, the family place named in the 1529 Cracow faculty record
sources: Cracow faculty record, 1529, transcribed in Rafal Wojcik, Opusculum, 80; quoted in The Art of Memory in Late Medieval Central Europe (2016), 303, 307
Ossolineum / Dolnoslaska Biblioteka Cyfrowa authority record, 'Enclen de Cusa, Johannes (1480-)'

stops.name: Cologne, the degree that travels with him
stops.date_confidence: undated: the mastership is attested by two later registers, at Ingolstadt in 1517 and Cracow in 1529, neither of which says when it was taken
stops.campa: He takes his mastership at Cologne, and the title travels with him for the rest of his life. Registers at Ingolstadt in 1517 and at Cracow in 1529 both put Coloniensis after his name, a generation apart and six hundred miles between them. What he studies in the largest arts faculty north of the Alps is not recorded. He leaves with a licence to teach. Artificial memory, the ordering of places and images, stands in no statute and on no syllabus; it is taught for cash outside the curriculum, term by term, by men who move on.
suggested_refs: The arts faculty of the University of Cologne, c. 1500
sources: Cracow faculty record, 1529 ('magister Coloniensis')
Matriculation entry, University of Ingolstadt, 6 May 1517, Die Matrikel der Ludwig-Maximilians-Universitat, Bd. 1, 407

stops.name: Cologne, the memory text of Henricus Vibicetus
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the Vibicetus material is associated with Cologne 'from around 1500' in the 2016 critical edition, reached here only through secondary summary
stops.campa: A treatise on artificial memory is circulating in the Cologne schools under the hand of Henricus Vibicetus. Its opening words will turn up again, unchanged, at the head of the little treatise printed at Frankfurt an der Oder in 1510 over the name of Johannes Cusanus. Whether the two men meet, whether one teaches the other, whether Vibicetus is dead by the time the text goes to press: the record answers none of it. Vibicetus himself is a name and nothing further: no birth, no post, no second book, no notice of his death, and no line written by anyone who says they knew him.
suggested_refs: The bracketed dual attribution '[Henricus Vibicetus-Johannes Cusanus]' in the 2016 critical edition
sources: Kiss and Wojcik, '[Henricus Vibicetus-Johannes Cusanus]: Tractatulus artificiose memorie,' in The Art of Memory in Late Medieval Central Europe (2016), 303-310, via secondary summary (pages not directly reachable)

stops.name: Cologne, the golden little work that does not survive
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the edition is known from bibliographic record only and rests on secondary summary of the 2016 critical edition
stops.campa: A press at Cologne issues the Aureum reminiscendi memorandique prebreve opusculum, a short golden work on remembering, carrying a prefatory epigram by the humanist Hermann von dem Busche. The epigram is signed and the text is not, so for a time the book is read as Busche's own, though he supplied only the verse. No copy is known today. The whole case against Cusanus rests on the incipit: the same words will open the treatise he prints under his own name nine years later at Frankfurt an der Oder. The edition itself survives as a catalogue line.
suggested_refs: Aureum reminiscendi memorandique prebreve opusculum (Cologne, 1501), no copy known
sources: Kiss and Wojcik (2016), 303-310, via secondary summary
Wojcik, 'Masters, Pupils, Friends, and Thieves,' Daphnis 41 (2012): 399-418, abstract and search-summarised excerpts (full text 403 Forbidden)

stops.name: Cologne, the first year of the wandering
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed from his own two datings: the twenty-second year of the peregrinatio in 1523 and the twenty-seventh in 1529, both counting back to 1501 or 1502
stops.campa: By his own reckoning, entered twice in print, the road begins here. At Lubeck in 1523 he dates a preface to the twenty-second year of his wandering out of love of philosophical learning; at Cracow in 1529 he calls it the twenty-seventh. Counted back, both land on 1501 or 1502. He takes the word peregrinatio in its scholar's sense, a road walked from university to university, and he will walk it, by his own account, through seven kingdoms. What he leaves behind at Cologne, and why, and whether he means ever to stop, he never sets down.
suggested_refs: The prefaces of 1523 and 1529, in which he numbers the years of his own peregrinatio
sources: Johannes Cusanus, Textus lecture arborum consanguinitatis (Lubeck: Vitus Blancken, 1523), f. 1v, quoted in the 2016 volume, 304 n.5, 307
Johannes Cusanus, Textus lecture quatuor arborum (Cracow: Scharffenberg, 1529), f. 1v, quoted in the 2016 volume, 307 n.28

stops.name: Zwolle, the press of Arnold Kempen
stops.date_confidence: attested: the imprint is dated 20 October 1502
stops.campa: On the twentieth of October the press of Arnold Kempen at Zwolle finishes a new arithmetic under the name Johannes Enclen de Cusa: Algorismus proiectilium de integris novus. It is his first surviving book and it has nothing to do with memory. The memory treatise printed at Cologne the year before does not survive; this one does. The pairing holds for the rest of his working life, mnemonics and arithmetic carried together. Neither trade needs a library or a chair, only a room, a board, and students willing to pay at the door.
suggested_refs: Johannes Enclen de Cusa, Algorismus proiectilium de integris novus (Zwolle: Arnold Kempen, 20 October 1502)
sources: A. J. E. M. Smeur, 'Johannes Enclen de Cusa en zijn Algorismus Proiectilium, Zwolle 1502,' Scientiarum Historia 4 (1962): 63-75 (cited, not obtained)
Albrecht Heeffer, study of Georgius de Hungaria, logica.ugent.be/albrecht/georgius.pdf, p. 4, listing the 1502 Zwolle imprint as extant

stops.name: Zwolle, counters thrown on a ruled board
stops.date_confidence: attested for the imprint; the description of the method is the standard sense of the genre title, not read off the book itself
stops.campa: The projectiles of the title are jetons, small cast counters thrown onto lines ruled across a table, each line a place and each place a power of ten. A merchant's son learns to lay them out, carry them up a line, sweep them off, and read the answer off the board. Counters and memory-places run on one principle, a place that holds a value until it is called for. Whether he ever says so himself cannot be known. The Zwolle book has been studied once, in a Dutch article of 1962, and is otherwise unread.
suggested_refs: Reckoning-counters and the ruled reckoning board of the German and Netherlandish schools, c. 1500
sources: A. J. E. M. Smeur, Scientiarum Historia 4 (1962): 63-75
Farkas Gabor Kiss, 'Classroom Commentaries,' Central European Cultures 2, no. 1 (2022): 54, on his teaching of mnemonics and arithmetic

segments.name: Frankfurt an der Oder: the Little Treatise

stops.name: Frankfurt an der Oder, a university four years old
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1510 imprint; no document places him personally in the town
stops.campa: The Viadrina opened on the twenty-sixth of April 1506, the first university in the Margraviate of Brandenburg, chartered by Elector Joachim I with the permission of Pope Julius II. It is four years old and short of nearly everything a university needs, above all cheap Latin books its students can buy and mark up. Into that gap arrives a treatise on artificial memory and a printer willing to set it. Here the little treatise first exists as a physical object, with a title page, a printer's name on it and a price.
suggested_refs: The Alma Mater Viadrina at Frankfurt an der Oder, opened 26 April 1506
sources: Kiss, 'Classroom Commentaries' (2022), 54
Standard history of the Viadrina (charter 1506, Elector Joachim I, Pope Julius II)

stops.name: Frankfurt an der Oder, printed by Johann Hanaw
stops.date_confidence: attested: the imprint is dated 1510. One footnote in the 2016 volume gives the printer as unnamed, another names Hanaw; the contradiction is left standing
stops.campa: Johann Hanaw, printing at Frankfurt an der Oder from 1509, sets the sheets. The title is a market notice rather than a scholar's heading: a little treatise on artificial memory, quite useful and necessary for students of any age whatever. It names no faculty, claims no doctrine, and addresses anyone of any age who can pay for the course the book advertises. The modern editors normalise its spelling, cuiuscunque for cuiuscumque, admodum for admodis. The first sheet off Hanaw's press has them as they stand here.
stops.quote: Tractatulus artificiose memorie omnibus cuiuscumque etatis studiosis admodisque utilis et necessarius
stops.quote_source: Title page, Tractatulus artificiose memorie (Impressus Francophordie ad Oderam: per Joannem Hanaw, 1510), recorded in The Art of Memory in Late Medieval Central Europe (2016), 304 n.9
suggested_refs: The 1510 editio princeps of the Tractatulus artificiose memorie, Frankfurt an der Oder
sources: 2016 volume, 304 n.9 (title page); 144 n.114 (same imprint given as 's.t.', no printer named); 311 (critical text, normalised spelling)
Deutsche Biographie, Johann Hanau, printer at Frankfurt an der Oder 1509-1528 (sfz25782)

stops.name: Frankfurt an der Oder, Cicero on the first folio
stops.date_confidence: attested for the printed epigraph; its position on f. 1r-1v is recorded in the 2016 volume
stops.campa: Before a word of his own, he prints Cicero. The passage is from the second book of De oratore, where Antonius reports having seen Carneades at Athens and Metrodorus of Scepsis in Asia, men who said they set down whatever they wished to keep as though in letters upon wax, by images placed in places. His students at Frankfurt read that before they read anything he wrote. A few pages earlier in that same book stands the banquet at Crannon, the roof coming down on the guests, and Simonides of Ceos naming the crushed by where each had reclined.
stops.quote: Vidi ego summos homines et diuina prope memoria Athenis Carneadem, in Asia, quem viuere hodie aiunt Sceptium Metrodorum, quorum uterque tanquam litteris in cera, sic se aiebat imaginibus in his locis, quos haberet que meminisse vellet prescribere.
stops.quote_source: Cicero, De oratore 2.88, printed by Johannes Cusanus on f. 1r-1v of the Tractatulus artificiose memorie (Frankfurt an der Oder, 1510); quoted in The Art of Memory in Late Medieval Central Europe (2016), 144 n.114
suggested_refs: Cicero, De oratore, book 2, the banquet at Crannon and the invention of the method of loci
sources: 2016 volume, 144 n.114 (Kiss, 'The art of memory in Hungary'); the critical text at 311 prints 'in Asiam' for 'in Asia' under the rubric 'Cicero artis detractoribus', a variant recorded and not resolved

stops.name: Frankfurt an der Oder, the pupil's epigram
stops.date_confidence: attested: the signed epigram stands on f. 1v of the 1510 edition
stops.campa: On the verso of the first leaf a pupil signs a verse in his master's honour: Eberhard Verberius of Gdansk, hearer of the artificial memory of Master Johannes Cusanus. A teacher selling a course by subscription puts his customers in the window. Two further humanists, Hermann von dem Busche and Hermann Trebelius, supply epigrams to the tradition, though no source consulted here says which edition carries which. In this printing the master's own name is set in small letters, less prominent on the page than the names of the men praising him.
stops.quote: Eberhardus Verberius Dantiscus auditor artificiose memorie M. Joannis Cusani.
stops.quote_source: Epigram signature, Tractatulus artificiose memorie (Frankfurt an der Oder, 1510), f. 1v; quoted in The Art of Memory in Late Medieval Central Europe (2016), 304 n.11
suggested_refs: The epigrams of Eberhard Verberius, Hermann von dem Busche and Hermann Trebelius attached to the Tractatulus
sources: Secondary summary of the 2016 edition's front matter naming the three epigrammatists, without a per-edition breakdown [R]

stops.name: Frankfurt an der Oder, the greatest and the lesser places
stops.date_confidence: the content is undated and is localised only by the imprint that first carries it
stops.campa: The system divides space before it stores anything. Loci maximi, loci maiores, loci minores: a greatest place, which is a building or a quarter of a town; within it the larger places, its rooms; within those the lesser, a window bay, the corner of a chest, a step down to a cellar. Each smallest place takes one image and holds it. The tiering is not his. It is already standing in the memory treatises of the previous century, numbered and walkable and fit to be dictated to a room in an hour, and he takes it as he finds it.
suggested_refs: The tiered loci maximi, maiores and minores of the fifteenth-century memory treatises
sources: Kiss and Wojcik (2016), via secondary summary of Wojcik, 'Masters, Pupils, Friends, and Thieves'

stops.name: Frankfurt an der Oder, the alphabet copied from Publicius
stops.date_confidence: the borrowing is undated; it is fixed only by the printing that carries it
stops.campa: The alphabet the treatise supplies, letters and numerals rendered as images to be planted in the places, is copied from the woodcuts of Jacobus Publicius, whose Ars memorativa had been printed at Toulouse and at Paris in the 1470s and again at Venice by Erhard Ratdolt in 1482. Word for word, in the judgement of the scholar who later collates them five centuries afterwards. Nothing on the page marks the borrowing, and a student buying the treatise at Frankfurt has no way to learn of it. Publicius is nowhere named in the printed text.
suggested_refs: Jacobus Publicius, Oratoriae artis epitomata (Venice: Erhard Ratdolt, 1482), with the woodcut mnemonic alphabet
sources: Wojcik, 'Masters, Pupils, Friends, and Thieves,' Daphnis 41 (2012): 399-418
AUC Philologica 2020/2, 'Iacobus Publicius's Ars memorativa: An Approach to the History of the (Printed) Text,' 85ff., for the Toulouse c.1475-76 and Paris c.1475-80 editions

stops.name: Frankfurt an der Oder, the rival alphabet laid on top
stops.date_confidence: the borrowing is undated; it is fixed only by the printing that carries it
stops.campa: Onto the same pages he lays a second image-alphabet, the one Conrad Celtis had published in his Epitoma in utramque Ciceronis rhetoricam. Celtis had rejected Publicius's method outright and said so in print. Cusanus copies both men and reconciles neither, so that a student working through the treatise is handed two rival sets of images for the same letters with nothing in the text to say which to use. Celtis had died at Vienna on the fourth of February 1508, two years before the book appears.
suggested_refs: Conrad Celtis, Epitoma in utramque Ciceronis rhetoricam, with its mnemonic alphabet
sources: Wojcik, Daphnis 41 (2012), via search-summarised excerpt
AUC Philologica 2020/2, on Celtis among the critics of Publicius
Celtis's death at Vienna, 4 February 1508: AEIOU Osterreich-Lexikon

stops.name: Vienna, the city of the second alphabet
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the 1514 printing is attested, but no document places Cusanus himself in Vienna or gives him a post there
stops.campa: The treatise comes to Vienna, where Celtis had taught until his death and where the Collegium poetarum et mathematicorum, founded by Maximilian I in 1501 at Celtis's urging, had installed poetry, rhetoric and the mathematical arts inside the university with four endowed chairs. What is recorded is that his book is set and sold here, in the market another man had made, and that a copy of it reaches a student who writes down what it cost him. Whether Cusanus holds any position in the town, or is ever in it at all, no document that could be read will say.
suggested_refs: The Collegium poetarum et mathematicorum, Vienna, founded 1501 by Maximilian I at Conrad Celtis's initiative
sources: AEIOU Osterreich-Lexikon and Wien Geschichte Wiki, Collegium poetarum et mathematicorum
University of Vienna, '650 plus' history project
Kiss, 'Classroom Commentaries' (2022), 54, for the itinerant career [the Vienna teaching itself is unattested, R]

stops.name: Vienna, Vietor and Singriener set the second edition
stops.date_confidence: attested: the imprint is dated 1514 and named in Kiss's bibliography
stops.campa: Hieronymus Vietor and Johann Singriener, partners supplying the University of Vienna with its classroom texts, print the treatise a second time. It repeats, without saying so, the opening words of the Cologne opusculum of thirteen years before, of which no copy is left to compare it against. This is the printing that survives best. One copy sits today in the Hungarian National Library at Budapest under the shelfmark Ant. 10008; another, bought and annotated by a Bavarian student, will end its travels in the ducal library at Wolfenbuttel.
suggested_refs: Tractatulus artificiose memorie (Vienna: Hieronymus Vietor and Johannes Singrenius, 1514)
sources: Kiss, 'Classroom Commentaries' (2022), 54-55 and bibliography 74
Budapest, Hungarian National Library, Ant. 10008
Wolfenbuttel, Herzog August Bibliothek, A: 104.11 Quod. (5)

stops.name: Vienna, the sermon built by fives
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1514 text at f. B1v-B2r; the scheme itself is undated
stops.campa: The working heart of the method is a group of five, and the customers for it are preachers. To build a sermon, he instructs, set the words of the theme at the head of one group of five places; put the exposition and the allegories at the places of that same five; then divide the sermon into its members, set each member at the head of a further five in order, and the remaining places stand open for the authorities to be cited under each. He is reworking an older anonymous scheme, the Memoria fecunda, which had divided by three.
stops.quote: Volens facere sermonem, locet primo verba thematis ad principium quinarii. Deductionem vero siue declarationem eiusdem et allegationes ad loca eiusdem quinarii: quo facto diuidat intentionem suam et quodlibet membrum diuisionis istius locet ad principium vnius quinarii secundum ordinem et sic patebunt loca pro autoritatibus adducendis: et pro quolibet membro subdiuidendo.
stops.quote_source: Johannes Cusanus, Tractatulus artificiose memorie (Vienna: Vietor and Singrenius, 1514), f. B1v-B2r; quoted in The Art of Memory in Late Medieval Central Europe (2016), 153 n.139
suggested_refs: The anonymous Memoria fecunda, the threefold scheme Cusanus reworks into fives

stops.name: Vienna, the woodcut that explains nothing
stops.date_confidence: attested for the printed woodcuts and the annotated copy; the annotations themselves are undated
stops.campa: The woodcuts printed with the treatise do not explain themselves. A reader who owns the book and has not sat in the room cannot work out from the page what the diagrams are for. The images are laid out and left unglossed, and the gap between them and the text is where the fee lives. In the Budapest copy at folio a3r a student has filled the margins in his own hand, headed a note De auctoritatibus et allegationibus, and written imagines again and again down the side of the printed lines. Others bound extra sheets into their copies to hold what the master said aloud.
suggested_refs: Budapest, Hungarian National Library, Ant. 10008, f. a3r, woodcut with student marginalia
sources: Kiss, 'Classroom Commentaries' (2022), 54 and 55, fig. 3 and caption

segments.name: Ingolstadt and Leipzig: the Fee and the Third Printing

stops.name: Ingolstadt, entered in the register
stops.date_confidence: attested: matriculation dated 6 May 1517
stops.campa: On the sixth of May the University of Ingolstadt enters him under the rector Martinus Otingensis and the vice-rector Johannes Eck. It is the first document that puts his body in a named town on a named day. The line has been read as of Trier, in the diocese of Cologne, which no map allows; the Cracow entry of 1529 unpicks it the other way, a man of the diocese of Trier who took his mastership at Cologne. He matriculates as any student would, in a university with no chair for what he sells, so that he may teach it lawfully inside the walls for as long as he stays.
stops.quote_source: Matriculation entry, University of Ingolstadt, 6 May 1517, in Die Matrikel der Ludwig-Maximilians-Universitat, Ingolstadt, Landshut, Munchen, Bd. 1, ed. Polnitz and Wolff (Munich, 1937), 407; quoted in the 2016 volume, 305 n.16
suggested_refs: The matriculation register of the University of Ingolstadt, rectorate of Martinus Otingensis, 1517
sources: Die Matrikel der Ludwig-Maximilians-Universitat, Bd. 1, 407
Cracow faculty record, 1529, for the alternative parsing of the name form

stops.name: Ingolstadt, three talents for the hearing
stops.date_confidence: attested: the year 1517 stands inside the student's own note. The place is supplied by Cusanus's Ingolstadt registration in the same year
stops.campa: A student named Georg Jobst buys the Vienna edition, takes the course, and writes across his own copy what it cost him: in the year of the Lord 1517 I heard this treatise on artificial memory from master Johannes Cusanus, a man far from unlearned, for which hearing I gave three talents. What Jobst paid for was the part that was never printed, and the note survives only because he wrote it into the margin of the part that was. Three pounds is a serious price for a course of lectures; the printed book he wrote it in cost a fraction of that.
stops.quote: Anno Domini millesimo Quingentesimo decimo septimo hunc audivi de memoria artificiosa tractatum a magistro Joanne Cusano viro haud inerudito de quo tria dedi talenta audiendi.
stops.quote_source: Marginal note by Georg Jobst the Elder in his copy of the Tractatulus artificiose memorie (Vienna, 1514), Wolfenbuttel, Herzog August Bibliothek, A: 104.11 Quod. (5); quoted in the 2016 volume, 306 n.18
suggested_refs: Georg Jobst the Elder's annotated copy, Wolfenbuttel, Herzog August Bibliothek, A: 104.11 Quod. (5)
sources: Kiss, 'Classroom Commentaries' (2022), 54

stops.name: Leipzig, the third printing
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the Leipzig 1519 edition is named only in search summaries of the 2016 critical edition. Kiss's 2022 article, read in full, names only Frankfurt an der Oder 1510 and Vienna 1514
stops.campa: A third edition is recorded at Leipzig, the fair town of the German book trade, where a manual of this kind can travel further than either university press had carried it. The evidence is thinner here than anywhere else in the print history: the edition is named in the modern scholarship on the treatise, but the one article that catalogues his printings mentions only Frankfurt an der Oder and Vienna, and lists only Vienna in its bibliography. Whether Cusanus is anywhere near the town when the sheets are set, nothing says.
suggested_refs: The Leipzig book fair and the university press quarter, 1519
sources: Kiss and Wojcik (2016), 303-310, via secondary summary [R]
Kiss, 'Classroom Commentaries' (2022), 54 and 74, which do not mention Leipzig

stops.name: Lubeck, the four trees of kinship
stops.date_confidence: attested: the imprint is dated 1523
stops.campa: Twenty-one years out from Zwolle he surfaces at Lubeck, where Vitus Blancken prints his Textus lecture arborum consanguinitatis, affinitatis, cognationis spiritualis et legalis, a schoolbook on the four trees of kinship: blood, marriage, godparentage, adoption. It is the first of his books in which he stands at the front and claims the thing outright, twenty-two years and at least four presses after he began. The preface opens with a greeting to the pious reader in his own name.
stops.quote_source: Johannes Cusanus, Textus lecture arborum consanguinitatis, affinitatis, cognationis spiritualis et legalis (Lubeck: Vitus Blancken, 1523), f. 1v; quoted in the 2016 volume, 307
suggested_refs: Textus lecture arborum consanguinitatis (Lubeck: Vitus Blancken, 1523)
sources: 2016 volume, 307

stops.name: Lubeck, the twenty-second year
stops.date_confidence: attested: the dating stands on f. 1v of the 1523 preface
stops.campa: He dates the same preface twice over, once by the calendar and once by his own road: in the year 1523 after the virgin birth, the twenty-second year of his wandering out of love of philosophical learning. Both datings stand on the same leaf as his greeting to the pious reader. The count he keeps is of years spent moving, and he keeps it the way a religious keeps years in an order. No university employs him. No patron is named anywhere in the sheet, and no city in it is called home.
stops.quote: Anno post virgineum partum Millequingentesimo vicesimotercio Anno peregrinationis sue philosophice amore scientiae vicesimosecundo.
stops.quote_source: Johannes Cusanus, Textus lecture arborum consanguinitatis (Lubeck, 1523), f. 1v; quoted in the 2016 volume, 304 n.5, 307
suggested_refs: The Lubeck preface of 1523, in which he numbers the years of his peregrinatio
sources: 2016 volume, 304 n.5 and 307

stops.name: Copenhagen, enrolled and licensed to teach
stops.date_confidence: attested: enrolled 9 October 1524 per the Copenhagen matricula
stops.campa: On the ninth of October the university at Copenhagen enrols him and admits him to teach: the measure of the four trees of consanguinity, affinity, spiritual kinship and legal kinship, together with the measure of artificial memory. Two subjects, one licence, granted to a master of the diocese of Trier who has arrived at the gate with a printed book for each. The entry survives because a scholar at Flensburg copied out the old Copenhagen matricula and had it printed in 1734.
stops.quote: Anno 1524. Mag. Johannes Cusanus Trevirensis Dioeces. fuit inscriptus 9. Octobr. et admissus ad communicandam mensuram quatuor arborum Consanguinitatis, affinitatis, cognationis spiritualis et cognationis legalis, una cum mensura memoriae artificialis.
stops.quote_source: Matricula Academiae Hafniensis, transcribed in Albertus Thura, Regiae Academiae Hafniensis infantia et pueritia sub tenebris pontificiis (Flensburg: Korte, 1734), 37; quoted in the 2016 volume, 307 n.24
suggested_refs: The matricula of the University of Copenhagen, entry of 9 October 1524
sources: Albertus Thura, Regiae Academiae Hafniensis infantia et pueritia (1734), 37

stops.name: Copenhagen, one word for both trades
stops.date_confidence: attested for the wording of the entry; the reading of it is this file's own
stops.campa: Mensura is the word the clerk chooses for both, the measure of the trees and the measure of artificial memory. Kinship laid out on a branching diagram and a house laid out in places are one operation performed on different material: a thing too large to be held is drawn as a space, and then the space is walked. He has been selling that operation since Zwolle, in three trades and across half a dozen kingdoms. Nothing in his own surviving prose says he ever put it that way himself.
suggested_refs: The paired licence at Copenhagen, kinship trees and artificial memory under one word
sources: Matricula Academiae Hafniensis, in Thura (1734), 37, quoted in the 2016 volume, 307 n.24
Kiss, 'Classroom Commentaries' (2022), 54

segments.name: Cracow: the Last Entry, and the Brackets in the Title

stops.name: Cracow, the Szarfenberg press
stops.date_confidence: attested: the imprint is dated 1529
stops.campa: Maciej Szarfenberg prints at Cracow, for the publisher Marek Szarfenberg, the Textus lecture quatuor arborum consanguinitatis, affinitatis, cognationis spiritualis ac legalis, under the name Johannes Enclen de Cusa. It is the Lubeck book again, reset for a Polish market six years and several hundred miles later. Its catalogue record carries the only birth year anyone has ever given him. It is the last book any press prints for him. A copy is in the Ossolineum collection under the shelfmark XVI.Qu.2347.
suggested_refs: Textus lecture quatuor arborum (Cracow: Maciej Szarfenberg for Marek Szarfenberg, 1529), Ossolineum sig. XVI.Qu.2347

stops.name: Cracow, nineteen universities and seven kingdoms
stops.date_confidence: attested: the entry stands in the Cracow faculty record for 1529
stops.campa: The faculty at Cracow writes him into its record in full, and this is the fullest he ever gets: Johannes Kusanus, son of Petrus Henklen of Kues, of the diocese of Trier, master of Cologne, lecturer in artificial memory in nineteen universities and seven kingdoms. Nineteen and seven are his own figures, given to a clerk by a man near the end of a long road. Five of the nineteen can be named from surviving documents and two more can be guessed from imprints. The other twelve are a claim, and nobody has ever checked it.
stops.quote: Johannes Kusanus Petri Henklen de Kusan d. Triverensis, magister Coloniensis..., Lector artificiose memorie in decem novem Universitatibus et septem regnis.
stops.quote_source: University of Cracow faculty records, 1529, transcribed in Rafal Wojcik, Opusculum, 80; quoted in The Art of Memory in Late Medieval Central Europe (2016), 303, 307
suggested_refs: The Cracow faculty record of 1529, the fullest surviving statement of his name and career
sources: Wojcik, Opusculum, 80, via the 2016 volume, 303 and 307

stops.name: Cracow, the twenty-seventh year
stops.date_confidence: attested: the dating stands on f. 1v of the 1529 preface
stops.campa: He dates the Cracow preface as he had dated the Lubeck one, in the twenty-seventh year of his wandering, out of love of philosophical learning. It is the last sentence anyone has from him in his own voice. Five years have gone by since Lubeck and the count has advanced by exactly five, which means he has not stopped anywhere long enough to consider himself arrived. He is about forty-nine, if the birth year a cataloguer assigned him holds, and he has been walking since he was roughly twenty-two.
stops.quote: Anno vero peregrinationis suae, amore scientiae philosophicae, vigesimo septimo.
stops.quote_source: Johannes Cusanus, Textus lecture quatuor arborum consanguinitatis (Cracow: Scharffenberg, 1529), f. 1v; quoted in The Art of Memory in Late Medieval Central Europe (2016), 307 n.28
suggested_refs: The Cracow preface of 1529, the last dated statement in his own voice

stops.name: Cracow, the four trees as a walked diagram
stops.date_confidence: attested for the book; the reading of the trees as a mnemonic device is inference, stated by no source
stops.campa: The four trees are drawn rather than argued. Consanguinity climbs from a common stock through grandparents and cousins; affinity, spiritual kinship and legal kinship each take a tree of their own, the degrees hung on branches so that a canonist can find an impediment to a marriage by running a finger up a line. A student who has bought both of his courses is being taught one habit twice over: give the material a shape, then keep the shape. No source says the connection was ever his intention.
suggested_refs: The arbor consanguinitatis and arbor affinitatis of the canon-law schoolbooks
sources: Dolnoslaska Biblioteka Cyfrowa catalogue record for the 1529 Cracow print

stops.name: Cracow, where the record stops
stops.date_confidence: the last dated attestation is 1529; nothing after it has been found, and the closing date is a marker rather than an event
stops.campa: After 1529 there is nothing. No death entry, no grave, no portrait, no will, no further university. The name Enclen de Cusa appears on no other title page, and no chronicler in any of the seven kingdoms notes his passing. A man who spent twenty-seven years arriving in towns leaves no record of the last one. What is left of him is what students bought: three printings of the memory treatise, two of the kinship trees, one arithmetic from Zwolle. The men who paid to hear the rest of it out loud wrote some of it into their margins, and those copies are at Budapest and Wolfenbuttel.
suggested_refs: The absence of any post-1529 attestation under either name form
sources: Absence across Kiss (2022), the 2016 volume as quoted, Wojcik (2012) abstract, and library catalogue searches under Cusanus, Kusanus and Enclen de Cusa

stops.name: Budapest, the brackets in the title
stops.date_confidence: attested: the volume was published in 2016
stops.campa: Five centuries on, the little treatise is edited from the surviving copies and printed again, one of ten memory texts out of Bohemia, Hungary and Poland brought together in a volume issued at Budapest and Paris. On the contents page the work carries two authors inside a single bracket, Henricus Vibicetus and Johannes Cusanus, because the editors cannot choose between the incipit that points back to Cologne and the three title pages that say Cusanus and nothing else. Their judgement on what lies between the covers is not gentle.
stops.quote: an interesting example of a borrowing, or indeed, a theft of ideas conceived by his predecessors, in some instances transformed, in some others, simply plagiarized
stops.quote_source: Rafal Wojcik, 'Masters, Pupils, Friends, and Thieves: A Fashion of Ars memorativa in the Environment of the Early German Humanists,' Daphnis 41 (2012): 399-418, on the Tractatulus

stops.name: Budapest, the company he is edited into
stops.date_confidence: attested for the scholarly roster; any direct borrowing between the named authors is not asserted by the sources
stops.campa: The same scholarship sets him in a roster of the men who worked this trade between about 1474 and 1530: Matheolus Perusinus, Jacobus Publicius, Conrad Celtis, Petrus de Ravenna, Jodocus Wetzdorf, Conrad Umhauser, Hermann von dem Busche, Johannes Cusanus. Masters, pupils, friends and thieves, the article calls them, a circuit of short printed manuals composed, compiled and lifted from one another at the university-town presses. Cusanus enters that market nineteen years late, with a book of other men's alphabets, and sells it in seven kingdoms. Peter of Ravenna had opened it in 1491 with his Phoenix.
suggested_refs: Petrus de Ravenna, Phoenix, sive artificiosa memoria (1491), the first printed memory-training manual
